source_table: Results, 'Hematology' paragraph 1; Supplementary Figure S5a
notes: QUALITATIVE ROW - no numerator is printed. Source text verbatim: 'In nonGLP screening studies we have evaluated ~ 40 2'MOE chimeric ASOs at a dose of 40 mg/kg/wk and identified only a few ASOs that produced sustained effects on platelet counts (see Supplementary Figure S5a). Thus, there is no apparent class effect on platelets, but individual sequences may be problematic in the NHP and perhaps humans.' The visual floor is an approximate reading of an unlabelled plot and is recorded as context only, not as a value. Exposure duration TBD; Fig S5a x-axis runs from study day -20 to about day 93.

effect_vs_control: antiparallel beta sheet 24.2% (PF4 alone) -> 35.8% with 5 ug/mL aptamer; heparin at 6.9 ug/mL gave 34.3%
source_table: Fig 5A (values in Results, 'Aptamer-induced changes in PF4 resemble those induced by heparin')
notes: Text: 'Deconvolution of the spectra of PF4 obtained after the addition of 5 ug/mL 44mer-DNA protein C aptamer or 6.9 ug/mL heparin showed an increase in anti-parallel b sheet content from 24.2% to 34.3% for heparin and to 35.8% for the 44mer-DNA protein C aptamer. This refolding was balanced by a decrease of the a helix fraction from 12.2% to 8.9% (heparin) and to 8.1% (44mer) and a decrease in the b-turn fraction from 22.8% to 19.8% (heparin) and 20.5% (44mer). Parallel b sheet and random coil content did not change significantly.' Most pronounced alterations over a broader aptamer range (5-20 ug/mL) than heparin (6.9-7.2 ug/mL). Cell-free mechanistic row: this is the neoepitope-forming conformational change, but NO platelet endpoint was measured, so grade 0 per the convention applied to all cell-free rows here. DISCREPANCY: Methods states PF4 at 40 ug/mL for CD; the Fig 5A legend states PF4 at 20 ug/mL.

notes: Fig 5B-C legend: '44mer-DNA protein C aptamer (8 ug/mL, bar 7)'; HIPA titration range 0.05-1000 ug/mL. source_table: Abstract (Results)

Bruising was associated with a dose-dependent prolongation of clotting times, particularly activated partial thromboplastin times (APTT), that was transient in nature. source_table: Secondary Pharmacology, Applicant's Position, ex vivo megakaryopoiesis system (Mosoyan, 2017) narrative (printed p47)
notes: Published ex-vivo work cited by the Applicant and concurred with by FDA: 'imetelstat affected normal megakaryopoiesis solely by delaying MK precursor maturation, and such effect was reversible upon drug withdrawal ... This may account for one of the potential mechanisms of imetelstat-induced, reversible thrombocytopenia in patients.' Graded 2 (megakaryocyte effect). No concentration or magnitude is given in the review - both TBD. This maturation-delay-plus-reversibility mechanism is the nonclinical counterpart of the clinical finding that 86.3% of Grade 3/4 events resolve within 4 weeks.

effect_vs_control: significantly inhibited vs untreated control at >=3.75 uM; no numeric magnitude printed
source_table: Secondary Pharmacology, FDA's Assessment, Study No. GRN01 narrative (printed p47)
notes: THE MECHANISTIC ROW. Normal human bone marrow cells treated with 0, 0.9, 1.875, 3.75, 7.5 or 15 uM imetelstat; 'significantly inhibited the number of MK colony growth at >= 3.75 uM'. readout_value TBD because no colony counts or percentages are printed (Applicant Figure 1 is a bitmap). GRADED 2 PER THE IN-VITRO RUBRIC: a dose-dependent megakaryocyte effect at a CLINICALLY RELEVANT concentration. Exposure anchor computed from the review's own unit conversions: the document equates 750 ug/mL with ~150 uM (printed p48), giving ~5 ug per umol, so the popPK-predicted human Cmax of 89.2 ug/mL at the approved 7.1 mg/kg dose is ~18 uM - the 3.75 uM threshold is roughly 0.2x total human Cmax, i.e. BELOW therapeutic plasma concentration, not supra-clinical. This is the direct mechanistic explanation for the clinical thrombocytopenia and is telomerase/megakaryopoiesis-driven, not phosphorothioate platelet binding.

effect_vs_control: no inhibition of erythroid or myeloid colony number up to 15 uM
source_table: Secondary Pharmacology, FDA's Assessment, Study No. GRN01 narrative (printed p47)
notes: NEGATIVE CONTROL / LINEAGE-SELECTIVITY ROW - grade 0, is_platelet_specific FALSE (adjacent haematology kept for context). 'Imetelstat did not inhibit erythroid or myeloid colony number (although colony morphology was compromised at 15 uM), but significantly inhibited the number of MK colony growth at >= 3.75 uM.' The megakaryocyte lineage is selectively hit across the whole 0.9-15 uM range - this lineage selectivity in vitro is why thrombocytopenia (94% at the recommended dose) tracks so closely with, and slightly exceeds, the other cytopenias clinically.

effect_vs_control: decrease in large (>50 cell) MK colonies vs control; no numeric magnitude printed
source_table: Secondary Pharmacology, FDA's Assessment, Study No. GRN05 narrative (printed p47)
notes: Follow-up to GRN01 using the same method and concentrations. Large colonies (>50 cells) 'resemble the progeny of the most primitive MK progenitor cells with a high proliferative potential' and are DECREASED at >=7.5 uM - imetelstat depletes the most primitive, highest-proliferative-potential megakaryocyte progenitors, which is the compartment whose loss produces a sustained platelet plateau rather than a transient dip. Graded 2 (dose-dependent megakaryocyte effect at a concentration below/near human Cmax ~18 uM). readout_value TBD - no counts printed.

effect_vs_control: increase in small (2-20 cell) MK colonies vs control; no numeric magnitude printed
source_table: Secondary Pharmacology, FDA's Assessment, Study No. GRN05 narrative (printed p47)

source_table: Combined Clinical/Biostatistical Review sec 4.4 'Nonclinical Pharmacology/Toxicology' (PDF p17)
notes: CROSS-SPECIES EXPOSURE-MARGIN row. Verbatim: 'Safety margins based on AUCs at the no observed adverse effect levels (NOAELs) for severe thrombocytopenia in monkeys and kidney toxicity in rats were <= ~2-fold, suggesting monitoring in humans may be warranted.' Graded 3 because the severe (fatal-in-animals) thrombocytopenia NOAEL sits at or below ~2x the human clinical AUC - i.e. the severe effect occurs at essentially clinical exposure, which is the animal analogue of the rubric's grade-3 'at or below therapeutic plasma concentration' criterion. Human reference exposure: Cmax 12.1 ug/mL at 300 mg SC weekly.

source_table: Combined Clinical/Biostatistical Review sec 4.4 'Nonclinical Pharmacology/Toxicology' (PDF p17)
notes: 39-week monkey study, LOW-DOSE BAND. Verbatim: 'five other animals across the three lowest dose groups showed perivascular mixed cell infiltration in multiple organs ... and (in 4/5 animals) with moderate reductions in platelet counts (49-70%, compared to baseline).' So 4 of 5 animals in the three lowest dose groups had moderate platelet reductions. Grade 2 (source's own word: 'moderate'). Numeric mg/kg doses not stated in this document -> TBD. Together with the severe cases in the two highest dose groups this establishes a dose-response across the monkey study.

source_table: Results, SAFETY, paragraph 3: 'No cases of thrombocytopenia with platelet counts of less than 50,000 per cubic millimeter occurred after the institution of weekly platelet monitoring'
notes: EXPLICIT ZERO, and it is evidence. Had events occurred in this band (<50x10^9/L) the row would have carried grade 3; it is recorded as grade 0 so the severe band stays findable. Important interpretation: this zero measures the effect of a risk-mitigation protocol (weekly platelet monitoring plus dose-stopping rules), not an absence of intrinsic hazard -- the same compound produced three <25x10^9/L events before monitoring was intensified. Graded on the severity of the underlying event (<25x10^9/L, grade 3) -- reversibility does not downgrade an event that was life-threatening while it lasted, and one of the three did not recover. source_table: Discussion, paragraph added during manuscript review
notes: QUALITATIVE ROW - no event count, no platelet value, no dose is given. Source text verbatim: 'During the review of this manuscript, we reported that severe thrombocytopenic events occurred in two placebo-controlled phase 3 studies with two different 2'MOE chimeric ASOs, IONIS-TTRRx and volanesorsen... we have never previously experienced severe thrombocytopenic events in any clinical trial including long term studies. While these trials remain blinded and investigations to understand the causes of these events are still in progress, we do know that the events are not due to prolonged exposure as all events occurred 4-9 months after initiation of therapy.' Graded 3 on the authors' explicit characterisation 'severe thrombocytopenic events'. IMPORTANT CAVEAT for downstream use: the trials were still BLINDED at time of writing, so drug attribution was not established in this source; the authors flag infections, concomitant drugs and the underlying diseases as possible contributors. This row is the phase-3 counterpart to the null healthy-volunteer result in Table 2 and is the single most consequential statement in the article for this endpoint.

notes: HUMAN clinical row — the priority class for this dataset. One subject in the Phase I programme had a platelet decrease explicitly described as reversible. GRADING RATIONALE (non-obvious, please read): the abstract gives NO platelet count, no nadir, no percent decline, no denominator and no route/dose attribution, so the grade rests only on the qualitative descriptors available. Grade 1 is assigned because the event is stated to be reversible, no intervention, dose interruption, dose reduction, bleeding or discontinuation is described, and the paper's own conclusion is that the drug was "generally well tolerated intravenously and subcutaneously". Grade 1 should be treated as a FLOOR, not a confirmed ceiling: if the full text (inaccessible - see extraction_notes) shows a count in the 50-99 x10^9/L band or a dose interruption, this row becomes grade 2, and grade 3 if <50 x10^9/L or antibody-mediated. dose_or_conc_value/unit are TBD rather than the printed 0.1-6 mg/kg i.v. band because the abstract does not say whether the affected subject was in the i.v. escalation or an s.c. cohort - assigning the band would be an invented attribution. readout_unit is n_subjects rather than pct_incidence because the abstract states no total N, so an incidence percentage cannot be computed without fabrication. EXCLUSION LINE: ISIS 104838 targets TNF-alpha mRNA and has no intended antiplatelet or antithrombotic pharmacology, so this platelet decrease is an UNINTENDED effect and is correctly in scope; none of the on-target-antithrombotic exclusion (ARC1779 / pegnivacogin class) applies here.

notes: Regulatory bottom line: thrombocytopenia is listed as a monkey (M/F) finding with NOAEL 10 mg/kg qw and only a 3x clinical safety margin. dose_or_conc_value recorded as the band '>10' verbatim in spirit (the finding occurred above the NOAEL, i.e. at 30 mg/kg qw, the only higher dose tested). Safety-margin basis per footnote a: body-mass scaling for toxicity judged to arise from intravascular/Cmax-related exposures, body-surface-area scaling otherwise; elsewhere the review calls 30 mg/kg/week '~10x clinical exposure' (BSA-scaled), so the two multiples are consistent under different scalings. SPECIES-TRANSLATION CONTRAST: the approved human Kynamro label carries no thrombocytopenia warning, while this 1-year monkey study did.

notes: ADJACENT row (is_platelet_specific FALSE) kept because it bears directly on whether the monkey thrombocytopenia was antibody-mediated. Anti-mipomersen (anti-drug) antibodies, NOT anti-platelet antibodies - no anti-platelet antibody assay was performed anywhere in this review. As printed: 'all samples with positive binding activity were found to be of very low titer (1:100). It seems unlikely that these low titer antibodies materially affected the study or contributed to any of the toxicity findings noted above.' Grade 0 on the platelet endpoint. NB the specificity table does show ADA-positive samples in animals 5007 (Days 185, 269) and 5506 (Days 185, 269), i.e. the two most thrombocytopenic monkeys, but the reviewer discounts a causal role on titer grounds. The review's own preferred mechanism is complement-mediated platelet activation/consumption plus splenic sequestration, with acquired haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) considered: monkeys #5505 and #5506 'had evidence of immune-mediated (macrophage/histiocyte) extravascular destruction of RBCs and/or platelets, and may also have had an HLH-like syndrome' (review p82).

source_table: Discussion, p540-541 narrative ('a classic heparin-induced mechanism for thrombocytopenia was excluded, as were antisense-mediated effects on platelet production')
notes: MECHANISTIC NEGATIVE — grade 0. A production-side (megakaryocyte) mechanism was excluded, pointing to peripheral platelet clearance instead. IMPORTANT LIMITATION: this is a bare assertion in the Discussion; the paper describes NO assay, criteria, bone-marrow examination or supporting data for the exclusion and cites no reference for it, so readout_value is the qualitative word 'excluded' and effect_vs_control is TBD. tissue is recorded as bone_marrow because that is the compartment the claim concerns, but no bone-marrow sampling is reported. CONVERGENCE ACROSS SOURCES: this agrees with the independent EMA EPAR finding of no haematopoietic/bone-marrow toxicity in cynomolgus monkeys, so two independent documents concur that the mechanism is peripheral rather than central — a useful human-to-animal extrapolation anchor.

source_table: Discussion, p540-541 narrative ('Nearly all the patients received an injection of heparin at the beginning of the trial and at approximately 26 weeks to enable measurement of LPL activity, but a classic heparin-induced mechanism for thrombocytopenia was excluded')
notes: MECHANISTIC NEGATIVE — grade 0, and an important confounder-exclusion specific to this trial. Nearly all patients received heparin TWICE (at baseline and ~week 26) because post-heparin LPL activity was an eligibility/assessment measure, creating a genuine risk that heparin-induced thrombocytopenia would be mistaken for drug-induced thrombocytopenia; the authors state classic HIT was excluded. LIMITATION: no anti-PF4/heparin antibody assay, 4T score, timing analysis or other criteria are described and no data are shown, so readout_value is the qualitative word 'excluded'. Recorded because ruling out HIT is what licenses attributing the platelet signal to the oligonucleotide itself. Note that PF4 is the antigen in classic HIT and PS-oligonucleotide/PF4 interaction is a known mechanism of interest for this endpoint, but this paper does not address that possibility.

source_table: Discussion, p540-541 narrative ('The underlying mechanisms responsible for the declines in platelet levels are not clear at present... There was some evidence for associated immunologic response in the most severe events')
notes: QUALITATIVE MECHANISTIC ROW, graded 3 on the severity of the events it refers to (the CTCAE grade-4 cases). GRADING CAVEAT STATED EXPLICITLY: this does NOT satisfy the rubric's 'immune-mediated thrombocytopenia with CONFIRMED anti-platelet antibodies' criterion, because NO anti-platelet antibody result of any kind is reported anywhere in this paper — the authors say only that there was 'some evidence for associated immunologic response', with no assay, titre, numbers or reference given, and they state plainly that the underlying mechanism 'is not clear at present'. readout_value therefore carries the source's hedged wording verbatim and effect_vs_control is TBD. This is the strongest support this paper offers for the rare, severe, immune-mediated limb of the endpoint's bimodal presentation, and it is weak; the two grade-4 patients' clinical response to glucocorticoids and IVIG is circumstantially consistent with an immune mechanism but is not presented as evidence by the authors. FOR CONTRAST, the EMA EPAR reports that anti-drug-antibody status did NOT increase the incidence of platelet decrease (78% ADA-negative vs 38% ADA-positive) and that anti-platelet antibodies were undetectable in 7 of 8 affected monkeys — both arguing against an antibody-mediated mechanism.
